case.label: B
case.text: A self-managed NFS server on EC2 keeps the application unchanged and works across both zones, but it adds patching, capacity and failover work, so it loses on the LEAST overhead constraint.

case.label: D
case.text: S3 is shared, durable and reachable from VPC-connected Lambda functions, but it is an object API, not standard file operations, so it fails the stated requirement.

case.label: C
case.text: An alarm plus Lambda that raises the file system size looks like automation of capacity, but EFS has no size to raise, so the option is invalid; the stem's own wording (does not want to plan, size or grow) points straight at EFS.

case.label: A
case.text: io2 Multi-Attach is block storage that SQL Server clusters can use for shared disks, but it is limited to one Availability Zone and gives no SMB share across two zones.

case.label: A
case.text: Provisioned throughput at peak level restores performance for sure, and a small 100 GiB file system makes the absolute cost modest, but paying for peak throughput all day while the application is idle most of the day is not the most cost-effective choice.

case.label: B
case.text: A Regional file system is the default and avoids cross-zone mounting if the Auto Scaling group spans several zones, and the stem does not say the group runs in a single zone; but the stem accepts loss of access in a zone outage, so the cheaper One Zone class fits.

case.label: D
case.text: EFS is shared and multi-AZ and grows automatically, but it speaks NFS only and cannot give SMB shares with Active Directory permissions to Windows Server.

case.label: C
case.text: A persistent Lustre file system linked to the bucket with backups protects the results against server failure, but the stem says a failed step can be repeated from S3, so the extra persistent cost is not needed.

answers.flag: Elastic throughput (D) is defensible because AWS presents it as the simple default for many workloads, and the stem gives no prices, so the Provisioned versus Elastic cost break-even for a steady near-peak load rests on outside pricing knowledge.

case.label: D
case.text: Elastic throughput restores performance at once with no sizing and no commitment, and a team could argue it costs the same or less than provisioning for the peak; but for sustained near-peak use the per-GB throughput charge makes Provisioned cheaper.

case.label: B
case.text: On the console the default policy is Auto, so B would be right for a volume made there; the stem names the CLI, and that detail (the CLI default is different) carries the question, which makes the key depend on one remembered default.

case.label: E
case.text: AWS Backup with cross-Region copy is a managed disaster recovery path with little operational work, but a daily plan gives an RPO of a day, not minutes, and the stem demands ongoing replication.

case.label: C
case.text: Cross-Region replication also survives an Availability Zone failure and adds Region-level protection, but it costs more and the stem only asks for zone-level availability, so B wins on cost.

case.label: A
case.text: A Lustre file system filled by DataSync gives the same throughput and a clear process, but copying 200 TB delays the start and wastes effort when each job reads only part of the data.

case.label: A
case.text: The Single-AZ 2 name suggests a newer, more resilient generation, but a Single-AZ file system stays in one zone, so the stated reason in the option is wrong.

case.label: D
case.text: FSx for OpenZFS is a ZFS-based NFS file system and could be argued as a lift and shift of volumes, but it is not ONTAP: it cannot receive NetApp SnapMirror replication or keep the ONTAP tools, and the SMB claim is doubtful.

case.label: B
case.text: Growing one file system in place is the simplest idea and works if one Windows file system could hold 300 TiB; it fails only because a single file system has a maximum size that the stem does not state, so the question tests a remembered limit.

case.label: A
case.text: Opening TCP 2049 to 0.0.0.0/0 would make the mount work, and the VPN limits who can reach private IPs in practice, but it is not the most secure choice when an exact address range is available.

case.label: A
case.text: Keeping everything in Standard avoids any latency or access charges on reopened projects, but it pays Standard price for months of cold data, so it is not the most cost-effective. Option C also repeats the phrase first access from the stem's reopened-project story, which is a mild wording cue.

case.label: C
case.text: AWS Managed Microsoft AD with a trust is the classic exam pattern for hybrid Active Directory, and a team could say it is the more standard design, but it adds a directory to run and pay for, which the LEAST operational overhead constraint rules out.

case.label: C
case.text: Sticky sessions send a user back to the instance that holds the reports with no code change, but colleagues who open a shared link are different users and the instance can be removed, so the failure stays.

case.label: B
case.text: The stem says durable block storage and io2 has higher durability and consistent latency, so B could be defended; but a moderate, steady load and the MOST cost-effective constraint point to gp3.

case.label: B
case.text: FSx for NetApp ONTAP also gives fast writable clones (FlexClone) and NFS, but the teams would have to change their ZFS snapshot and clone workflow and the stem says not to change it.
